newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Brazilians seen mopping up last Argentine wheat.
newsitem.headline: Brazilians seen mopping up last Argentine wheat.

text.p: Argentina's export sales of its 1996/97 wheat crop have reached between 8.5 million and nine million tonnes, with Brazil the biggest buyer and likely to take another million tonnes or so, traders said Wednesday.
"We think the Brazilians have bought about 3.5-4.0 million tonnes already, and they might take another 1.0-1.5 million tonnes," a trader told Reuters.
"Their ending stock last year was smaller than in other years, so they will probably want to buy a bit more than usual this time round," he added.
Another trader thought sales so far had only reached about 8.5 million tonnes, with the Brazilians responsible for three million tonnes of that.

Argentina's last sales of its 1996/97 crop are currently going through a patch of the dolldrums, with wheat offered at about $165 a tonne without freight for loading from mid-July to mid-August in the southern ports and about $5 more in Buenos Aires or upriver. Brazilian bids are about $8 cheaper.
"It's quiet. The Brazilians are bidding for pretty cheap prices, and with this rise in Chicago over the past few days, no one in Argentina is in any hurry to sell," a trader said.
Aggressive Canadian competition is providing some problems for the Argentines, particularly for delivery from September onwards, traders said.
"I think that as of September there'll be more demand for Canadian than for Argentine. One reason is the quality, we have a lot of poor quality wheat this year, another is the logistics," one said.

Argentina produced 16 million tonnes of wheat in 1996/97. But this record crop was marred by torrential late season rains which left about one million tonnes affected by sprouting and only serviceable as forrage.

This coming season's wheat is also facing some problems. A combination of price differentials tempting producers into other crops like soybeans and both too much and too little rain in the wrong places will cause a substantial fall in sown area from last season's 7.3 million hectares.
A very wet autumn and early winter in key Buenos Aires province and lingering drought in southern Santa Fe and Cordoba has also delayed sowing.

"Unfortunately the new crop isn't going too well," a trader said, "There are still places like Nueve de Julio in western Buenos Aires where the farmers haven't been able to get their machinery into the fields because of the water."
Traders forecast area to fall from 11-17 percent, and for production to be 12-13 million tonnes, given fairly normal conditions.
